Cnidaria. A phylum of radially symmetrical aquatic animals including jellyfish, corals, sea anemones, and hydras. They're characterized by specialized stinging cells called cnidocytes, which contain explosive organelles called nematocysts used to capture prey and defend against predators by injecting toxins.

Cnidarians exhibit radial symmetry and are diploblastic, developing from only two primary germ layers—ectoderm and endoderm—separated by a jelly-like layer called the mesoglea. They possess a simple tissue-level body plan and alternate between two main body plans. There's the stationary cylinder-shaped polyp and the free-swimming umbrella-shaped medusa. They feature a simple nerve net without a centralized brain, using only basic sensory receptors for light, gravity, and touch to navigate their environment.

The phylum includes siphonophores like the Portuguese man o' war, which are fascinating because they're not actually single organisms at all. They're colonies of specialized individual units called zooids working together.

Porifera is a simpler animal phylum that lacks the true tissues and symmetry found in cnidarians. Ctenophores are a similar phylum of gelatinous marine animals—the comb jellies—but they lack cnidocytes entirely, instead capturing prey with sticky cells.
